display.title: The Disappearing Sleeve
display.summary_short: An agunah asks the Koznitzer Maggid to find her missing husband. He shows him to her in a basin of water, and she pulls out the very sleeve he is pressing.
display.summary_long: The storyteller begins with video calls: a hundred years ago nobody would have believed you could see someone thousands of miles away, and it would sound even less possible to pass an object through a phone. Yet over two hundred years ago a tzaddik did something like it with ruach hakodesh. The story, from a book of stories the Frierdiker Rebbe gave to the Rebbe, is about the Koznitzer Maggid, a student of the Mezritcher Maggid. An agunah, whose husband vanished years ago and who cannot remarry without a get, comes with her brother for help. The Maggid has her look into a basin of water, where she sees a city, a marketplace and her husband among the tailors, pressing a sleeve. At the Maggid's word she reaches in and pulls out the sleeve, still warm. Trusting the tzaddik, the two set out without knowing where to go, find themselves left in a forest, and walk into the very city she saw. With the help of the local Rav and the sleeve, the husband can no longer deny who she is.
display.lesson: Tzaddikim can see and help with ruach hakodesh, and when we trust a tzaddik's words, Hashem leads us the right way.

advisories.note: A woman left an agunah for years; her husband had remarried in another town.

sources_cited.note: The story is 'written in a sefer called Sippurim Noraim', which the Frierdiker Rebbe gave the Rebbe as reliable.

segments.title: From video calls to ruach hakodesh
segments.summary: Today's technology helps us imagine what a tzaddik could do long ago.

segments.title: The Koznitzer Maggid and the sleeve
segments.summary: An agunah pulls her husband's sleeve out of a basin of water and finds him in a faraway city.

quality.notes: Source named on air: the sefer 'Sippurim Noraim' (no works id). ASR garbles Koznitz (Kajnitz, Koshnitz).

identity_guesses.evidence_quote: I believe in Hashem, I trust in Hashem. There never is a moment when that I am alone
